steps.text: Acetyl-CoA carries an activated two-carbon acetyl unit. It can arise from pyruvate oxidation, fatty-acid oxidation and some amino-acid pathways.
Citrate synthase combines acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate. Oxaloacetate is regenerated during the cycle, so its availability affects acetyl-unit oxidation.
Acetyl-CoA is also a precursor for fatty-acid synthesis and ketone production in appropriate compartments and metabolic states. A branch-point metabolite has several possible fates.
Human metabolism has no net conversion of acetyl-CoA carbon to glucose through the ordinary citric acid cycle. Regenerating oxaloacetate is not net synthesis of glucose carbon from acetyl units.

lessons.title: Reactions of the Citric Acid Cycle

steps.text: One cycle turn per acetyl-CoA produces three NADH, one FADH2 equivalent, one GTP or ATP and two CO2 while regenerating oxaloacetate.
Oxidative decarboxylations occur at isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Incoming acetyl carbons are not necessarily the first carbons released as CO2.
Succinate dehydrogenase is also respiratory complex II in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Most other cycle enzymes are in the mitochondrial matrix.
The cycle supplies biosynthetic intermediates as well as reducing equivalents. Anaplerotic reactions replenish intermediates withdrawn for other uses.

steps.text: Electrons from NADH enter at complex I; electrons associated with succinate oxidation enter at complex II. Ubiquinone and cytochrome c carry electrons between complexes.
Complexes I, III and IV contribute to proton pumping from matrix to intermembrane space. Complex II transfers electrons without directly pumping protons.
Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor at complex IV and is reduced to water. Blocking electron transfer can limit NADH reoxidation and upstream oxidative metabolism.
The diagram is a qualitative electron-transfer organization, not measured current or molecular structure. Electron motion and proton movement are distinct linked events.

steps.text: Electron transfer establishes a proton-motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Protons return toward the matrix through ATP synthase to support ATP production.
An uncoupler dissipates the proton gradient without directly making ATP. When substrates and oxygen are available, respiration can increase even while ATP yield falls.
An ATP-synthase inhibitor blocks productive proton return; respiratory electron flow often slows as the gradient builds. This differs from proton leakage through an uncoupler.
Common ATP estimates use about 2.5 ATP per mitochondrial NADH and 1.5 per FADH2 equivalent, with assumptions. Whole-glucose yields vary with shuttles, transport costs and coupling.
